title: Sharing Our Maturity
speaker: Shin-yu Scott Allen
summary: Maturity is not just about acquiring skills and responsibilities, but also cultivating a deeper sense of spirituality that provides meaning and direction in life. This spiritual aspect is essential for leaving a positive impact on the world and making a difference in society. By acknowledging and working with our ego and its tendency to block personal growth, we can mature and develop a deeper understanding of ourselves and others, ultimately creating positive change through intergenerational connections and mentorship.

sentences.text: It's kind of like a rowboat, dharma talk, isn't it?
Wheels and gizmos.
This month I've been talking about maturity, and it's based on Norm Fisher's book, Taking Our Places.
In his book he talks about his conversation with four adolescents, 10 to 14 years old, who are just thinking about becoming adults.
Some of the things he talks about are really interesting.
My idea was, instead of talking about youngsters, to talk about us and whether some of those principles pertain to our lives.
I've talked about some of these things before in my classes, but today I wanted to take some of the points I hadn't brought up before, and some of the things I thought needed re-emphasizing.
The folks sitting here, I really think they're highly spiritual, and you're pretty mature mostly.
But you're the kind of people that, if you were asked, "Is that all there is?"
I remember a song years and years ago called "Is That All There Is," and that rattled around in my head for quite a while.
I'm sure if I asked you that, you would probably say, yes, and it's okay, it's all right.
And that is truly growth.

It struck me in the first chapters of the book that we have a situation where four families are asking Norm Fisher to help mentor their sons, because they didn't feel they were able to handle teenagers, I guess, and they needed the help.
I had to ask myself, why would that be?
These people are their parents.
If anybody would be able to mentor their own children, it should be their parents.
But such was not the case.
They needed outside help.
I thought, is this because the parents never got that kind of attention themselves, or didn't they have the time?
Because I think most of them were professional people.
That's pretty radical.
I think back on my life, and maybe it wasn't so radical after all, because my conversations with my father were skimpy at best.
I never got those kinds of conversations.
I remember I got one note when I went through some Air Force training.
My dad didn't write letters, and it said, "Son, I'm proud of you."
I cut that out of the note, put film over both sides of it, and kept it in my wallet until I wore it out, because that was the only time he had ever said that.
So maybe that's not so far-fetched after all.
Maybe he didn't get the nurturing from his father and mother.
I don't know too much about him.
He never talked about him, but I know my grandfather was a dark coal miner, a real gruff man.
He came to the house once to stay for a while, and all of us stayed away from him because he was a scary man.
He smoked two packs of [unclear: "palm oil"] a day, and he also had black lung.
It wasn't too much fun for him, I'm sure.
I'll be talking about people whom we already consider adults, you guys.
You have gained many of the basic lessons in dealing with life over the years.
You've paid the rent, done your taxes.
But how should we look at maturity for us?
Is there a place in society?
There are a lot of younger folks in here, and a lot of older folks, but it's applicable to both.
How do we take our place in society as adults?
What job is there?
What skills do we need?
Well, my basic thrust for this talk was very, very simple.
I believe that for us to continue to mature at any age, some things have to happen.
A lot of them we talk about in the [unclear: "Star Maw"].
We have to meet life head on, meet our challenges, continue to learn about ourselves, grow personally.
That's kind of a given.
But I'm going to add something else to it.
I think what we need to do is to be able to pass this knowledge and wisdom to those people that might benefit from it.
Sounds real simple, but sometimes the hardest things in life sound simple.
Well, we've got two groups of people: youngsters, let's call them less skilled, and then people that have more skills in life.
But what's the difference between the two groups?
None, really.
The teenagers are trying to gain those skills to be able to fit into society, make a contribution.
And isn't that what we want to do, too?
We're right in the middle of society, and we want to find our place, on a beautiful Saturday morning when you guys should be out hiking in the woods or something.
You're doing the hard work and listening to a dharma talk.
The goals of maturity encompass a lot of things that were in the book.
We talked about all kinds of chapters in there: responsibility, realism, right action, experience, self-acceptance, stability.
We talked about our vows and strength.
But Norm also talked about spirituality.
He said that we need both in our life.
We need the skill set that society wants us to have, but we also need the spiritual side of life, which includes faith in others and yourself, idealism, sense of self.
He talked about some of the tools that were necessary to make that happen, which were persistence, meditation, connection with others, attention, faith, and equanimity.
Spirituality is really essential to live a mature life.
It took me a lot of years to figure that one out.
I don't think I broke into that until my early 40s, because up to that time, spirituality did not really play a large part in my life.
I was one of those kids that as soon as they left home, that was the last time I went to church until I got married, and that was just a drive-by.
Maybe that's the wrong word for it.
Oh, never mind.
It felt a lot longer than that.
But I was late to the game, is what I'm trying to say.
I came to realize a few years later that the spiritual part really completed me.
It gave me that long vision and that faith that I needed to really enjoy a beautiful day like this.
Maturity centers, like I said earlier, on making a living, having a family, providing, meeting society.
But this spiritual life gives us meaning and a moral compass for our lives.
This is where we really have the edge over some of the younger guys.
That spiritual side gives us that moral compass, gives us long-term goals.
We're not thinking next week or even next month.
We tend to think of things like [unclear: "the Trinity"], you know, the rest of my life.

I feel it's necessary for our good and the good of society that we face our challenges, like I said before, correct those things we can, make amends for any wrong, but most importantly pass all those lessons on to other people.

It's also a great opportunity to revisit some of those issues that we may not have paid much attention to when we were in our teens and early twenties, when we just kind of shot right past them and said, oh, they're not that important.
I'll get to that stuff later.
For right now, I need to get this job, get this apartment, pay these bills, buy a ring, do all those kinds of things.
But I'll get to that someday.

I found that later in life, as I got a little bit more spiritual and my life started coming together in ways it hadn't before, I learned that there were some things I thought I should have gotten in Life 101 that I didn't get.
It's really humbling to look at some of those issues and take another look at them.
I've heard people say that it's really a bear going through puberty when you're 40.
And it is.
It really is.
Those things we thought we had?
Not so much.
But if we don't do something about it, at some point in our lives they're going to bug us at the least, or they'll cause us pain in various quantities, which is really a bummer.
Here's an analogy.
You have a river, one of those vast, [unclear: "semi-types"] of rivers with the smooth rocks in the bottom, crystal clear water.
I assume it's still crystal clear.
I haven't been back there in a while.
Somebody takes a rough rock and throws it into the stream, and it goes to the bottom and settles.
Over time, the top face of that rock that's exposed to the water becomes smooth, and it looks like all the other rocks.
But the downside is, you turn the rock over, and it's still rough.
That's kind of like dodging some of those issues.
We can also work with spiritual principles to gain a better understanding of life's meanings and our sense of self.
There are those questions again: Who am I?
Why am I here?
What do I need to do with the rest of my life?
We're the only people really that are in a position to do that kind of legwork.
We've already done the one-on-one courses, or most of them, and now it's time to do the junior and senior level courses.
And for a sense of meaning, how about this?
We take those lessons that we're learning for ourselves, and when the opportunity presents itself, [unclear: "have so long to another person"].
I had an experience late in my Air Force career.

I was on a flight, doing a route check on a crew flying into Bosnia and Herzegovina during the war, and my job was to make sure that they knew all the rules and some of the safety protocols that were in place.
On the way back, one of the engines started overheating, and we made the next landing at Frankfurt, Germany.

I suggested to the aircraft commander, a guy named Taz, a heavy-set guy, dark hair, big wide shoulders, like the Tasmanian Devil, but he was really a sweetheart, how we might fix that, kind of a Rube Goldberg type of fix to get us to the next place, 100 miles away, and get fixed.
I watched him interact with his engineer and his crew chief.
They did those things, and they talked amongst themselves, and they did the pros and cons, and they did it just exactly the way I would have done it, without me hardly saying a thing.
It dawned on me at that point that I had always thought nobody can do it as good as I can.
Not a chance.
I spent 12 years flying in Alaska, and you guys can't tell me a thing.
But this guy did it as good as I could have done it.
And I had a feeling at that point: maybe the world's in a pretty good place after all.
There are people that can take over, and I can retire with a good conscience about that.
I could have retired right on the spot with a big smile.
That's not the way it works, though, but I could.
We want to get more mature, and there's a pain factor.
But when we refuse, or don't want to, or don't know about certain problems, we [unclear: "start growing as adults"].
We talked about that [unclear: "teenager authority syndrome"], and some of us even block those things out, block out the suffering, and we can do it with all kinds of things.
We can do it with intoxicating substances.
We can do it with food.
My wife likes to do it with politics.
Our religion, too.
There are a lot of people that use my [unclear: "weird highway"] kind of religion to block everything else that doesn't agree with what they already think.
All we're doing there is sidestepping painful issues, and we're not growing.
And age is not maturity.
Two different things.
Looking at the book, and I hammered on this in my talks, a lot of this stuff in our [unclear: "soul"] boils down to an understanding of our true self, our ego.
That's been [unclear: "peaking me up"] for years.
And Buddhism talks about the ego.

We've got the three poisons: the grasping and clinging, the feeling that there's not enough and I want mine before somebody else gets it; the aversion and hatred, I want to hang on to what I've got and I'll defend it to the death; and delusion, not seeing things as they actually are.
All those things go back to ego.
It also can stunt our ability to take part in any group.
How many groups do you belong to other than this one?
Because this one's perfect.
Don't change a thing.
Where you have these little interplays of personalities, little infighting goes on, and usually that's due to people's ego.
I'm better than that guy, therefore I'm going to beat him up.
Or maybe I say I'm not worthy, I'm less than somebody else.
In either case, we're not fitting in.
We're not communicating.
We're really not part of the group.
Remember high school?
I went to my 50th reunion a couple of years ago, and it was amazing how mature my classmates had become.
Then again, it was me.
Do something about the ego.
If you're loaded with money, you can go to a shrink.
But the way most of us generally do that is we discuss our issues with a friend, a mentor, a support group.
I mentor two men here in Bellingham, and it's really a neat experience, because they can talk about something and I just sit back and listen to them.
Every once in a while I like to say something, and then I let them kind of go out on their own.
But there's a sense of helping.
It's really a good feeling.
Big Brothers is still around, Big Sisters.
I'm sure there are a lot of groups you can get involved with in the mentoring business.
But what we're really doing is learning those spiritual and maturity lessons, and we're passing them on to the [unclear: "Lutz Experience"].
This is really important in life, because first of all, everything that we have [unclear: "around Lutz, period"].
The only thing we're going to leave as a legacy of ourselves, if that's important to you, is the things that we've done to help or detract from other people.
And hopefully it's helped.
Those things are remembered, and passing on our life lessons is the best of those things.
I can give Bob my welder and he'll say thank you very much.
But the better gift is helping somebody out.
Bob doesn't need this.
He's mature.
Helping somebody out with their issues really is a source of great pleasure, and if you haven't done it, you might want to try it.
It's almost like the old throw-the-pebble-in-the-lake thing, and the concentric circles expand out.
It's kind of like that, because I've heard of people I've talked to telling the same thing to their friends.
I've used the term mentoring to describe many of the skills we were talking about earlier.
They include not only passing on useful knowledge that we've learned, but also offering kindness, friendship and useful suggestions.
Norm emphasizes that one of the skills that is absolutely critical is the ability to listen.
And it's tough.
It's tough with normal people talking, equals talking to each other.
We tend to do all those things I talked about earlier: interrupting, talking over somebody, thinking about what we're going to say in response to their talking.
He was trying to teach us to stop, listen completely to what they say, and then respond to it.
What's even harder is if you're talking with somebody that has less experience than we do.
I immediately want to jump in: well, I've done that before, and here's what you need to do.
It's kind of a be-reasonable, do-it-my-way attitude.
But what Norm teaches us is we have to sit and listen and let them come to their solution to the problem.
Give them a nod [unclear: "to read on them"] in the right direction, but they're the ones who are going to have to come up with a solution if it's going to work for them.
If enough seniors, or regular adults for that matter, did this, two things along this line, especially for seniors, it'll go a long way into upgrading some of our thoughts and some of our health.
We've kind of sidelined the elderly.
It used to be we had the wise grandmother or whatever, and I think Norm Fisher had a wise grandmother, I believe, and they had a good relationship.
But those kinds of relationships aren't as prevalent as they once were.
Sometimes you'll see these relationships between children and grandparents.
Grandparents have a little bit more time, a little bit more disposable income for their grandchildren.
There's no reason why we can't do that with people that are not our siblings, our children.
I don't know if you guys saw it, but there was a segment on NBC, I think, about a little boy, probably five years old, in the Midwest, and his next-door neighbor was a retired guy in his seventies.
He was riding a lawn mower, and that's a big sport there.
Somehow the little boy got a riding mower from him, the same John Deere, you know, green.
So when the man would go out and mow his lawn, the little boy would go out and mow his lawn.
This went on for a couple of years, and they developed a bond that was extremely tight, and it was an absolute joy to watch.
There was also a pain when the old man had to move away, go into a hospice, because, you know, it would get up.
But there was that connection.
You might think in your own mind, I'm not going to go into it, what are some of the ways that you right now can introduce some of the things that you know to other people?
Just food for thought.
This mentoring could give the experienced segments of our society more importance as contributing members, and also might help the fragmented family.
The grandparents can't always be there, but a neighbor can, even though the grandparents are 500 miles away.
Somebody can be there.
It takes a village, that attitude.
I think there's a lot of truth in that.
Teaching maturity and ethics would help the young learn those life lessons that we no longer teach in school.
We don't teach ethics.
I think very few parents might read Grimm's fairy tales to their kids.
We don't have a lot of the epic tales that we used to have in school.
That was where traditionally kids got a lot of their life lessons, from these teaching stories, and it would be good to reestablish that through the role of a mentor.
Also, it's really important not to force the issue, not to walk up to a kid and say, hey, kid, you need a [unclear: "veteran"].
It doesn't work like that.
But if the time and the circumstances permit, where [unclear: "the answered ask a question"] are stuck, that would be a real good time to practice.
It's obviously going to be more important to little girls than little boys, because little boys are taught real early that we don't follow directions.
We don't need any of that stuff.
And that's true.
Ever read Bray's book, Women from Mars?
No, Men from Mars, Women from Venus?
And he says right there, you can't tell a guy anything.
We won't open the instructions.
When we mentor another, our interactions will not only change the character of the person being mentored, but also benefit the maturity of everybody in here.
It serves as a mirror for those life lessons of ours that we might need to do a little bit more work on.
What started my journey on this whole project was a focus on Norm Fisher, and the question I asked him was a simple one.
Like I said, I don't ask for directions too much, because I know everything that should be known.
A lot of people are like that, I guess.
But his answer was to my question, how should my practice change with the events of the years?
His answer was, show more kindness and love.
And that is the mark of a truly mature person.
Thank you.
We've got a little bit of time.
Anybody have any questions?
Everybody here is mature.
I know I'm going to go out in the lobby and see a lot of mentoring going on.
No?
Okay.
Thanks for listening.
*Intentions deeply extend to every being and place.
Illusions are exhaustible.
I vow to end them.*
*Dharma gates are boundless.
I vow to enter them.
Life's unsurpassable.
I vow to*
